After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal.
  • Alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate.
  • The drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal. The treatment, called Zanvastro, represents a major advance for patients who previously had no options beyond managing their symptoms.

Alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate. Zanvastro is the first and only approved disease-modifying treatment for the condition, meaning it targets an underlying biological process responsible for the disease rather than simply relieving its effects.

The drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center. Much of that work took place in the laboratory of Albee Messing, professor emeritus of comparative biosciences and former director of the Waisman Center, whose discoveries helped make the treatment possible. Ionis Pharmaceuticals collaborated in developing the drug.

Clinical trials offered encouraging results. Patients receiving Zanvastro generally experienced stabilization of their motor function, and some showed improvements in their ability to move.

"This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community," Messing says.

Alexander Disease: A Rare and Devastating Brain Disorder.

Alexander disease affects fewer than one in every million people worldwide. Although exceptionally uncommon, its consequences can be severe, with symptoms that gradually interfere with everyday activities and essential bodily functions.

In a recent development, people with the disorder may develop seizures, lose previously acquired developmental abilities, experience increasing difficulty walking or moving, and struggle with speaking or swallowing. Some also develop dangerously elevated pressure inside the brain.

The disease does not follow a single predictable course. Symptoms may first emerge during infancy, childhood, or adulthood, and their severity and progression can differ depending on when the condition begins.

For decades, doctors could offer supportive care and treatments to ease individual symptoms, but they had no approved medication capable of targeting the disease itself.

An Unexpected Discovery Revealed the Genetic Cause.

Sources indicate that the breakthrough can be traced to research Messing conducted with Michael Brenner, professor emeritus of neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In the late 1990s, their work identified the genetic changes responsible for Alexander disease, providing scientists with a specific biological target for developing treatments.

The discovery began with an unexpected result in laboratory mice.

Messing and Brenner had genetically engineered mice to produce unusually high amounts of a protein known as glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). This protein is normally found in astrocytes, specialized cells that help support and maintain healthy function in the brain and spinal cord.

To the researchers' surprise, the modified mice developed abnormal protein deposits throughout their brains. These deposits appeared inside astrocytes and closely resembled the distinctive abnormalities seen in people with Alexander disease.

"We had, really without intending to, created a mouse that produced these classic lesions of Alexander disease," Messing says.

The abnormal deposits, called Rosenthal fibers, are a defining characteristic of the disorder. Additional genetic studies involving people diagnosed with Alexander disease confirmed that mutations in the gene responsible for producing GFAP were the underlying cause.

"This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy -- the GFAP protein," Messing explains.

It has been revealed that identifying the genetic cause also made diagnosing the condition much simpler. Instead of relying on invasive brain biopsies to look for characteristic tissue abnormalities, doctors could use genetic testing from a blood sample to identify the mutations associated with the disease.

Scientists Develop a Drug That Targets Harmful Protein Buildup.

Once researchers understood the role of GFAP, their next challenge was finding a way to reduce its production and prevent damaging levels of the protein from accumulating in brain cells.

It has been revealed that messing joined forces with Tracy Hagemann, an associate research professor at the Waisman Center, to create improved rodent models of Alexander disease. These models more closely reproduced important features of the disorder, giving scientists a way to investigate potential treatments before testing them in people.

The team focused on a straightforward idea: If excessive GFAP contributes to the disease, lowering the amount produced might help protect the nervous system.

In collaboration with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the researchers pursued a technology known as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs).

These treatments use short, specially designed pieces of genetic material to interfere with instructions that cells use to manufacture particular proteins. Rather than targeting every protein in a cell, an ASO can be designed to reduce production of a specific one.

For Alexander disease, that target was GFAP.

According to recent reports, the experimental treatment produced promising results in rodents, supporting the decision to move forward with human testing. A clinical trial began in the summer of 2021.

Zanvastro uses this same targeted strategy. By limiting GFAP production, the drug aims to reduce the buildup of the protein before it can cause additional damage.

Because the treatment needs to reach the central nervous system, it is administered through an injection into the spinal canal. A trained healthcare professional gives the injection once every three months.

Clinical Trials Show Improvements in Walking and Movement.

The human trial provided evidence that lowering GFAP could offer meaningful benefits to people living with Alexander disease.

Ionis Pharmaceuticals conducted the international study across 13 clinical sites, enrolling 54 patients to evaluate the treatment's safety and effectiveness.

After receiving Zanvastro for a little more than a year, treated patients demonstrated significantly better walking speeds than patients who had not received the drug.

The results also indicated that treatment could stabilize motor function, an important outcome for a progressive disorder that can steadily undermine a person's ability to move independently. Some participants experienced improvements in motor performance.

These findings helped establish Zanvastro as the first treatment approved to modify the underlying disease process in Alexander disease, rather than focusing exclusively on symptom relief.

The FDA approval covers people with Alexander disease across the full age spectrum, from infancy through adulthood.

Sources indicate that zanvastro is expected to become available in the United States in the weeks following the approval. Outside the United States, access to the drug will be handled through a licensing agreement between Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Recordati, a major pharmaceutical organization headquartered in Italy.

A 30-Year Scientific Journey Offers Newly introduced Hope.

For Messing and his colleagues, the approval represents the culmination of more than 30 years of research, beginning with basic investigations into brain cell biology and eventually leading to a treatment for patients.

What started as an unexpected finding in genetically modified mice helped reveal the cause of an extremely rare disease, transformed how doctors diagnose it, and provided the foundation for developing a drug.

The achievement is also an example of translational research, the process of turning discoveries made in laboratories into treatments that can directly benefit patients.

Throughout that journey, individuals living with Alexander disease and their families played an essential role by supporting the research and participating in studies.

"The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful," Messing claims.

According to recent reports, materials provided by University of Wisconsin-Madison. Original written by Charlene N. Rivera-Bonet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#45906. Industry News: Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2345 w)

Industry News: Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles.
  • Sources indicate that that’s just your teens becoming independent.
  • Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles. In the teen years, sweet hugs can provoke eye rolls; a well-intentioned “How was your day?” may be misconstrued as meddling.

Sources indicate that that’s just your teens becoming independent. Decades of research finds that portraying adolescence as a period of “storm and stress” is not only misguided, it’s harmful. In fact, developmental science indicates this time of life is better recast as “the breakthrough years.” According to research on over one thousand adolescents by Ellen Galinsky, author and president of Families and Work Institute, there are key messages that teens want to get through to adults:.

None of this is easy, of course. Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do. Here are common questions, with answers backed by scientists and their research.

It has been revealed that Q: My 16-year-old doesn’t seem to be motivated to do anything beyond hanging out with friends and playing video games. When I bring up the prospect of college, he says he doesn’t care. What should I do?

It has been revealed that A: As parents, we want to set our high schoolers up for success. But, at that age, young people are still trying to figure out who they are, what interests them, and what their future looks like. “Identity development and purpose formation are underway, but rarely fully formed by high school,” says Kendall Cotton Bronk, professor of psychology at Claremont Graduate University.

Not finding any answers yet is expected. “Parents need to remind themselves that where their child is at this moment in time isn’t necessarily where they will be in the future,” claims Bronk.

To help teens along, encourage them to try different activities at school and in the community, whether it’s, for instance, robotics, the debate team, chorus, improv, or the school paper. Leave it to them to select what to try. Don’t do it for them. Don’t judge their choices.

Recent findings suggest that “While it’s not appropriate for parents to be too directive, they can help their teenager reflect on what they liked and didn’t like and what felt meaningful and not so meaningful about their various experiences,” says Bronk. “Having someone to debrief with can help them deepen their reflection and more promptly identify a purposeful direction.”.

According to recent reports, research suggests that when teens are guided by their own interests, free of external pressures, they’re more likely to take charge of their own career development. But when parents are overly involved in their adolescents’ lives, claims Bronk, young people don’t have an opportunity to cultivate a sense of agency, and this can make career development planning a big challenge.

Recent findings suggest that instead of trying to manage their path, states Bronk, parents should simply “be curious.” Ask your child: What interests you? What feels satisfying for you?

According to recent reports, “This kind of questioning can scaffold and deepen their young person’s reflections, and reflection is a key component of figuring out what kind of path a young person wants to follow,” she says. “Usually, what holds their interest is something they’re good at and care about, and that allows them to make a meaningful difference in the broader world,” she explains.

Recent findings suggest that taking advantage of volunteer opportunities can help young people see themselves as useful and discover careers that might interest them—for instance, helping out in a food pantry, animal shelter, a kids sports organization, or hospital. Encourage your teen to ask people he knows about their jobs, what they entail, and what they studied to get there.

Finally, don’t assume that your child’s lack of direction is apathy. Whatever their interest is, “work with it, not against it,” states Bronk. “At the same time, be patient. It may just be the case that they haven’t figured it all out yet. Their timetable may not be the same as yours, but they will eventually get there. Remember, this isn’t a race.”.

It has been revealed that Q: My 15-year-old seems to be living a separate life. He spends most of his time in his room and has dinner more often with his friends than with us. How can we encourage him to be a part of the family?

A: Seeking independence (while still navigating being dependent on adults) is one of the primary tasks of adolescents as they transition to becoming more self-sufficient into early adulthood.

Industry observers note that “I try to get parents to understand that it’s not about them,” says Laurence Steinberg, author of You and Your Adolescent. “The parents didn’t do anything wrong; the child isn’t rejecting them. This is a sign they’re growing up normally. It’s partly wanting to make their own decisions and have their own life, but it’s also wanting emotional independence—to show that they are more than their parents’ kid.”.

Chances are a closed door doesn’t mean trouble. Just as most adults don’t want others listening in on their calls, teens don’t want that either. They’re not distancing themselves from you, but simply distancing themselves from being a child.

“There’s nothing the parents can do to stop this from happening,” says Steinberg, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. “And they shouldn’t try.”.

That said, spending time with family is also important. To suggest that, say something like, “We want to spend more time with you, but we also know that spending time with friends is important. What’s the best way to catch up with you?” By making the planning of it a collaborative process, your child is more likely to stay engaged. Research suggests that they may even find the activity more enjoyable.

According to recent reports, only rarely is a shut bedroom door cause for concern—for instance, you notice other behavioral changes, such as a drop in grades, a dwindling interest in his usual in-person activities. If you suspect an problem, let your child know that you’re there for him, and that he can get professional help, too.

Sources indicate that one last note: If your child is spending most of his time in his room online, setting limits on its own may not be enough, states Jacqueline Nesi, author of the Techno Sapiens newsletter and associate professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University. You’ll also want to discuss with them what you want for him and what he wants.

Industry observers note that the evidence also supports “co-viewing” or “co-using” technology with your kids, whether that’s a video game, TV, or an AI chatbot, claims Nesi. Using tech together can spark conversation and help parents better understand their kids’ digital lives.

That said, it’s still key for you to protect their sleep and to make sure that they live a life in person. Again, to get their buy-in, decide on screen-time parameters, and replace screen time with in-person activities he might enjoy, such cooking a favorite meal together or an outing with family and friends.

Q: My 17-year-old daughter recently suffered a breakup. How can I help her feel better without intruding?

Sources indicate that A: Even if a relationship doesn’t look like a monogamous romantic relationship in adulthood (it may be short, or the partners may not talk to each other very much), these breakups can still be painful. So always take your teen’s romantic activities seriously, as well as the emotions they are experiencing following a breakup, says Emily Bibby, a researcher at the Relationship Development Center at Stony Brook University. Be compassionate, validating, and nonjudgmental. Let her know that she is having a normal reaction to a difficult situation.

Industry observers note that allow space to grieve and vent. “Listen hard to what your child is thinking and feeling,” states Barry Farber, professor of psychology and education at Columbia University Teachers College. “Ask what they’ve learned from the relationship. Framing the relationship as a learning experience, as opposed to a failure, can help nurture resilience and personal growth, and can help her feel more in control and more hopeful about future relationships.”.

It has been revealed that as Farber and his coauthors point out in a recent study, while time doesn’t necessarily “heal all wounds” (because memories and thoughts can linger), it almost always “softens the blow” when other strategies are also employed, such as talking with a trusted friend or family member. While the study involved mostly white, female adult subjects, the same principle generally applies across ages, genders, and ethnicities. Letting your child know that things will get better can help.

Trying to convince a teen to do anything is difficult, indicates Farber, so it’s better to simply listen, and then only encourage as opposed to insisting or dictating. Encourage her to engage in activities she enjoys, whether it’s treating herself to an afternoon manicure, going to a concert, or spending time in nature like hiking and walking on the beach. Encourage her to avoid all contact with her ex, both in person and on social media. If one person believes it’s really over, a clean break is usually best, says Farber. Any surge of adrenaline that happens when you see your ex in any form is only temporary, and only makes it harder to get over the breakup.

Sources indicate that if sad feelings are impairing day-to-day life—she’s not seeing friends, she’s failing her classes, there’s a dramatic change in eating or sleeping—have her consider seeking help from a mental health professional. “Therapy normalizes the experience,” says Farber. “It helps people find a upcoming narrative when they’re stuck.”.

Therapy also gives people an opportunity to share their feelings in a private space and learn evidence-based emotion-regulation skills to improve their mental health and functioning, indicates Bibby.

This workbook is for a range of practitioners who support parents and caregivers of children between preschool and high school.

If your teen is debilitatingly depressed or harming herself, then advise that she get professional help as soon as possible, such as from her school psychologist, her primary care doctor (for a referral), or a therapist you think highly of.

To help their teen navigate relationships in general, parents can model healthy relationships with not just a partner, but also friends and family members. Teaching your teen effective communication skills and boundary setting early on, in the context of friendships and family relationships, can prove helpful once your teen starts dating, notes Bibby, who recently coauthored a research review on romantic relationships and mental health in adolescents.

According to recent reports, and as for parents of teens who are just becoming interested in dating, it’s helpful to talk about what healthy relationships look like, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect. “Thinking through what they would do [in different dating scenarios] and how to navigate different challenges that may arise can build confidence when they start dating,” claims Bibby.

Q: My 14-year-old has found herself in a friend group that spends a lot of money on expensive clothing and electronics. We don’t approve of these teens and don’t share their consumerist values. How do we prevent our child from becoming materialistic, too?

According to recent reports, A: You can empower your teen to make thoughtful, confident choices about money, friendships, and the pressures they face. Try leading with connection rather than control: Talk openly about your family’s values, help them practice setting boundaries, and remind them they do not need to match their friends’ spending to belong or feel worthy. Expensive tastes and social media pressures can be hard to ignore, but your teen can learn to make choices that reflect what matters most to them.

Recent findings suggest that people turn to materialistic things to fill a void, but that’s only a temporary fix, claims Lan Nguyen Chaplin, a professor of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University, and an expert in children’s and teens’ consumer behavior. “They end up in a vicious cycle of wanting and needing more to fill the same void because material things cannot fill real voids.”.

Industry observers note that in her research exploring materialism in a group of 12- to 18-year-olds, she reported that those with high self-esteem were less likely to have materialistic tendencies. “Parents and peers [are] a source of emotional support and psychological well-being,” she writes. “Supportive parents and peers boost adolescents’ self-esteem, which decreases their need to turn to material goods to develop positive self-perceptions.”.

Read this article in Spanish on La Red Hispana, the public-facing media outlet and distribution house of HCN, focused on educating, inspiring, and informing 40 million U.S. Hispanics.

Sources indicate that to that end, start at home and help your kids feel good about themselves. Gratitude journals can be a good way to curb materialism, but, of course, asking a teen who is new to journaling to start one can feel like a homework writing assignment if it’s yet another thing they are required to do. Rather, approach it with a light touch. Model gratitude by sharing with your teen who and what you’re grateful for, keep a gratitude journal yourself, or ask them what the high point of their day is.

Industry observers note that it also helps to stop tying accomplishments to material things. So, instead of, say, rewarding a good report card with money or sneakers, celebrate the hard work that was put into achieving the good grades over a fun experience together like a movie night at home.

Recent findings suggest that most of all, spend time with your teen in lighthearted and playful ways, no matter how short. Even a 10-minute car ride can be a good opportunity to connect with them, and also reinforce the good things they have going for them, Chaplin notes.

Joanne Chen is a writer and editor in Fresh York City. Her articles on children and parenting have appeared in The Bump, Parents Magazine, and the New York Times.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DixonBaxi rebuilt the CrazyGames brand identity around Ziggy, a purple cat with a voice, a type system and a world of his own.

CrazyGames is a free-to-play browser games platform, running since 2014. Millions of people knew the games, but almost nobody knew the brand, so DixonBaxi handed the whole identity to Ziggy, the cat-eared character who had been sitting in the corner of the site, unnoticed. Now he is the brand: a wide purple oval face, two heavy-lidded eyes, soft curves and a permanent look of mischief. The palette does the rest of the talking. Electric purple sits against acid lime and hot pink, with black fields that let the type shout. DixonBaxi unveiled the rebrand in October 2026.

It has been revealed that the type is set huge and stacked, three words filling the frame. FIND PLAY LOVE runs in pink, blue and purple capitals across a black field, with three small game cards tucked into the middle like a punchline. WORK. SCHMIRK. sits in blue over lime on a billboard, the period after each word doing the work of a full sentence.

Under the noise there is real construction. The icon is built from a wide oval face and soft curves, annotated on the case page like a piece of engineering, so the same face can go fuzzy, spiky, pixelated or cell shaded and still read as Ziggy.

Industry observers note that the system holds up in the physical world, which is where most character brands fall apart. Ziggy becomes a pendant on a ball chain, a purple handheld device with a pixel face, a plush toy, a giant inflatable installation with players inside, and posters on billboards and bus sides. One bus side reads: one day you will look back and wish you played more Crazy Games.

In a recent development, the voice lines keep the same tone everywhere, from the site to the street: Netflix can wait, curious people never get bored, I think I love it here. Player cards, the developer portal and the website all carry the same purple, the same lime, the same cat.

As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions.
  • It has been revealed that another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging.
  • In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center debuted the Newly introduced Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’” Carstensen was clear that the center’s aim was not to increase lifespans—which had nearly doubled during the 20th century—but rather to build societies that accommodated that fresh and unprecedented reality.

It has been revealed that another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging. As Carstensen noted often, “Longevity is not synonymous with aging. It is a metric of length.” The center’s interest is in the challenges and opportunities that longer lives present. While the center is keenly interested in older people, in Carstensen’s view, “longer lives have implications for every stage of life, and the roots of many problems faced at advanced ages have their roots much earlier in life.” The center’s mission is to use longer lives to improve quality of life at all ages.

In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center debuted the Newly introduced Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies. After nearly 20 years, Carstensen, the Fairleigh S. Dickinson Jr. Professor in Public Policy and a professor of psychology at Stanford, will step down this summer from her role at the Stanford Center on Longevity to pursue a new project alongside her research and teaching.

Sources indicate that I spoke with Carstensen about what she’s learned along the way and what’s next. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Karen Breslau: What’s changed since the center’s early days?

Recent findings suggest that laura Carstensen: I hope it’s clearer that the aging process has not changed much, if any, genetically over the last several thousand years. Rather, longevity—the length of life—increased, and that has enormous implications for nearly all aspects of our lives. The modifiability of aging, on the other hand, is also clear. Even though we’re essentially the same physiological beings that our ancestors were, we changed the world in ways that are allowing us to live healthier and longer. That’s why we are confident that we can build a world where the majority of people live well for a century.

Recent findings suggest that KB: You are on the scientific advisory council to the Health District of Singapore, which is building the Queenstown Health District, a very intentional all-ages community that is incorporating principles from the New Map of Life. What are you seeing?

Recent findings suggest that LC: The Singapore government has given a group of scientists the freedom to design a neighborhood in ways that support long-term health and intergenerational connections, continued financial security, and exercise. They’re thinking about all the factors that contribute to long, healthy, and engaged lives and literally programming them into the community. What’s really cool about the Queenstown Health District is that it can provide a proof of concept that social and physical designs can improve long life.

According to recent reports, already they have built parks and playgrounds with swings for the kids and balance beams for older residents, to provide shared spaces where different ages interact. When we advisers fly in from different countries, we’re starry-eyed at what they can do. Singapore can do things like this in part because they’re smaller, and their government can act quickly. For example, the government recognized about a decade ago that people weren’t saving enough for retirement. So they flipped a switch and mentioned, “OK, everybody’s putting in more money into their retirement account.”.

KB: If you had to give a grade to where the U.S. is in implementing the New Map of Life principles, could you take out your red pen?

In a recent development, LC: Compared to some countries, like Singapore, I’d give the U.S. a C-minus, and I am used to grade inflation! The federal government has done little to improve longevity. Unlike the Singapore government, which can require people to save more for retirement, for example, the U.S. cannot rapidly implement such programs. On the other hand, in part because the government contributes less, we see a lot of innovation coming from the private sector. We have entire industries offering latest products and services. So I’m optimistic about what the U.S. can contribute to longevity. At a global level, it’s fabulous to think about the different approaches that can come from the public and private sectors in a range of countries.

Sources indicate that KB: Longevity has gone mainstream and led to billions of dollars in market interest. How has that changed the center’s work?

LC: It’s true that vast investments are going to longevity. Most of these funds are directed at ways that individuals can live longer. There isn’t, in my experience, much philanthropic interest in this space aimed at helping people live better as we live longer lives. I am discouraged that we are sleepwalking through this seismic demographic shift without investing more in the opportunity to rewrite the life scripts that have guided life and imagining ways that we could use them to improve life.

It has been revealed that it’s also discouraging that as longevity has entered public consciousness, much of what we hear about are pitches for questionable products that supposedly make people live longer. There are so many snake-oil salesmen in this space that it’s hard for consumers to distinguish what is evidence-based and what is not.

Sources indicate that KB: As you often say, transitions are a feature of longer lives. What’s happening next for you?

LC: I’m going to focus more on research and teaching, but first I’m going on sabbatical and look forward to having more time for the things I love—my garden, being at home, sitting in the sun, going for walks. I want to take Pilates lessons. I’m going to take a break in my schedule to say, “How do I create a healthy lifestyle going forward and build the rest around it?”.

While I hopefully will have a more relaxed schedule, during my sabbatical I’ll be developing an online course called The Fundamentals of Longevity, which will tell the story of longevity and the potential to live longer, better lives, a change we really need in the world. The course will be accessible far beyond Stanford, so that we can help frame the conversation around longevity and help people appreciate the extraordinary promise of science, technology, and social change to improve life. There is a crisis on the horizon if we don’t change the way we live.

According to recent reports, we have the opportunity to change our lives for the better. We have opportunities no previous generation of humans in history has had, and we need to start implementing them.

Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, two people diagnosed with depression can experience vastly different symptoms.
  • Researchers at the University of Helsinki investigated this question and uncovered a striking finding: people with the same depression diagnosis can have dramatically different patterns of brain activity.
  • According to recent reports, depression is a major global health concern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, two people diagnosed with depression can experience vastly different symptoms. One might struggle with persistent anxiety and repetitive negative thoughts, while another may experience trauma related symptoms or substance abuse. But do these differences also appear in the way their brains function?

Researchers at the University of Helsinki investigated this question and uncovered a striking finding: people with the same depression diagnosis can have dramatically different patterns of brain activity. In some cases, communication between brain regions was unusually strong, while in others, it was weaker than normal.

According to recent reports, depression is a major global health concern. According to the World Health Organization (WHO, 2025), approximately 332 million (5.2%) adults worldwide are affected. In Finland, depression is the leading individual cause of both extended sick leave and disability pensions.

Brain Study Reveals Five Distinct Depression Profiles.

To investigate the biological differences associated with depression, researchers examined brain activity in 263 people diagnosed with major depressive disorder and 75 healthy participants who served as a comparison group.

Sources indicate that the analysis revealed five distinct groups based on differences in functional connectivity, a measure of how closely activity in different brain regions is coordinated. When two regions show synchronized activity, it suggests they are working together as part of a larger brain network. However, stronger connectivity does not necessarily mean the brain is functioning better.

In a recent development, "What was particularly interesting was the contrasting patterns of brain activity found under the umbrella of the same depression diagnoses. In some individuals, the functional connectivity between brain regions was stronger than usual, while in others it was weaker," indicates Director Satu Palva of the Neuroscience Center, University of Helsinki.

These differences were also associated with particular symptoms. Participants in one group indicated especially strong connections between brain regions, along with more pronounced substance abuse problems. Another group displayed weaker connections and a greater prominence of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that the contrasting results could help explain why earlier studies examining the brains of people with depression have sometimes reached conflicting conclusions. If researchers study different combinations of patients, they may observe very different patterns, even though everyone involved has received the same diagnosis.

Recent findings suggest that the findings add to growing evidence that depression may not have a single, consistent biological signature. Instead, the condition could involve several distinct patterns of brain function.

The Five Brain Patterns Linked to Depression.

The researchers classified participants with depression into five groups based on how strongly different brain areas communicated and the frequencies at which their activity was coordinated.

Each group had a characteristic pattern of brain connectivity and associated symptoms:.

Group 1: Strong connectivity and severe symptoms.

Participants generally indicated relatively strong connections between brain regions. This profile was associated with more severe symptoms across several areas, including depression, anxiety, rumination, and reduced ability to function in daily life. Rumination refers to repeatedly dwelling on distressing thoughts, worries, or negative experiences.

Group 2: Weaker connectivity and milder depression.

This group was characterized by relatively weak communication between brain regions. Compared with the other groups, participants generally experienced milder symptoms.

Group 3: Widespread weak connectivity and trauma symptoms.

In a recent development, people in this group showed reduced connectivity across substantial portions of the brain. Symptoms associated with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were particularly prominent.

Group 4: Mixed connectivity and multiple challenges.

It has been revealed that this profile combined unusually strong connections in some brain regions with weaker connections in others. Participants tended to experience more severe depression, greater substance abuse problems, and lower overall well-being.

Group 5: The strongest connectivity and substance abuse symptoms.

Sources indicate that participants in the fifth group had the strongest connections between brain regions of any group identified in the study. Substance abuse was a particularly prominent issue, while trauma related symptoms were less pronounced than in the other groups.

Importantly, all five groups also showed differences from the healthy participants. These distinctions extended beyond whether brain connections were strong or weak. The groups also differed in which brain regions were involved and the frequencies at which their activity was synchronized.

Together, the patterns suggest that people diagnosed with depression may experience substantially different changes in how their brain networks operate.

Measuring Brain Activity With Millisecond Precision.

To capture these differences, the scientists used magnetoencephalography (MEG), a brain imaging technique that detects extremely faint magnetic fields produced by electrical activity in the brain.

Unlike methods that track slower changes associated with brain activity, MEG can follow electrical signals as they unfold over extremely short periods. This makes it particularly useful for investigating the timing and coordination of communication between brain regions.

Using MEG, the researchers recorded brain activity in all 263 participants with depression and the 75 healthy control subjects.

"MEG enabled us to monitor electrical brain activity with millisecond precision, helping us get closer to what actually happens in the brain at any given moment. Previously, depression phenotypes have been studied using methods with slower responses," Palva notes.

This high level of temporal precision allowed the team to examine rapid changes in brain activity that might be difficult to distinguish using slower measurement techniques.

By studying these fast signals, the researchers were able to identify differences not only in the strength of connectivity but also in the frequencies at which brain regions appeared to work together.

Could Brain Activity Lead to More Personalized Depression Treatments?

The discovery raises an important possibility for the future of mental health care: treatments might eventually be selected partly according to a person's individual pattern of brain activity.

Today, finding an effective depression treatment can involve trying different medications or therapies and evaluating how well each works. Because patients can respond differently to the same treatment, identifying the most suitable approach is not always straightforward.

Industry observers note that brain activity measurements could eventually provide additional information to help guide these decisions. However, the researchers emphasize that their findings are not yet ready for clinical use.

"We're not yet at the point where brain measurements can be used to choose the right treatment for patients, but the study does show one possible route," Palva claims.

A major long-term goal is to better understand how particular symptoms relate to the way brain networks function. Connecting these biological patterns with patients' experiences could help researchers develop more precise ways to identify and characterize depression.

Eventually, such knowledge might allow doctors to determine which therapies are most likely to help individual patients, potentially reducing the amount of trial and error involved in treatment.

Sources indicate that for now, the five brain profiles offer a different way to understand depression. Rather than assuming that one diagnosis corresponds to one underlying pattern of brain activity, the findings suggest that depression can involve markedly different biological changes, sometimes even in opposite directions.

The research was carried out in collaboration with Aalto University and Helsinki and Uusimaa Hospital District (HUS).

Breaking: Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me.
  • Recent findings suggest that often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors.
  • Sources indicate that for the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Recent findings suggest that often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

Sources indicate that for the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

At Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

At Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

It has been revealed that back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Sources indicate that of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

It has been revealed that it’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins says these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”.

In a recent development, mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

It has been revealed that mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something fresh. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

Industry observers note that it was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty.

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible.

Recent findings suggest that as I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.

Sources indicate that in our Dickinson College episode, that choice indicates up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates. Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.

Sources indicate that the choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.

In a recent development, here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part.

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.

But the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur.

Sources indicate that I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

Recent findings suggest that at Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences.

The series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones.

In a recent development, in my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

Sources indicate that I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an issue than a conversation built only around agreement.

According to recent reports, lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

When Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates newly introduced points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

It has been revealed that at the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang.

According to recent reports, working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

For example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III.

If you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social concerns, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It demonstrates that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

Industry observers note that iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco.

Sources indicate that I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

As another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too vital to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

Industry News: Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, noted:.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

Could Firenze Lai’s first UK solo show signal a shift in global market recognition for Hong Kong artists?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In mid-October, coinciding with Frieze London and nearly four years after she relocated from her native Hong Kong to London, the artist Firenze Lai opened her first UK solo exhibition at White Cube Mason’s Yard.
  • Lai is among a handful of Hong Kong artists represented by major Western blue-chip galleries today.
  • The shift suggests the maturity of this generation of mid-career artists from Hong Kong, several of whom have relocated abroad fairly recently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In mid-October, coinciding with Frieze London and nearly four years after she relocated from her native Hong Kong to London, the artist Firenze Lai opened her first UK solo exhibition at White Cube Mason’s Yard. Featuring newly introduced works created in her adopted home, North and True North (until 14 November) is not just a milestone for her career, it also signals a potential shift in major galleries’ approach to Asia.

Lai is among a handful of Hong Kong artists represented by major Western blue-chip galleries today. Born in 1984 and educated in Hong Kong, the artist has exhibited internationally, including in the main exhibition of the 57th Venice Biennale in 2017. Her current show marks the first solo exhibition White Cube has staged by an artist originating from Hong Kong since it opened its outpost in the city in 2012.

The shift suggests the maturity of this generation of mid-career artists from Hong Kong, several of whom have relocated abroad fairly recently. It also raises hopes that Western blue-chip galleries are finally adopting a less siloed approach to Asia, in which global art markets were approached from a simplistic geographical perspective. This mindset of “keeping Asians in Asia” kept transnational relationships rare, the cultural strategist Adeline Ooi notes, but this is starting to change.

Recent findings suggest that “People are much more cosmopolitan and international today. They are not just rooted within their region and bounded by their geographies,” indicates Ooi, the former director for Asia at Art Basel.

It has been revealed that major international galleries are taking a more sophisticated approach, rather than simply placing Asian artists in front of Asian collectors, indicates the Taipei- and Upcoming York-based art adviser Gladys Lin. “It’s about integrating that artist into the wider language of the gallery programme, so that collectors from different backgrounds can understand the work in relation to other artists, histories and conversations.”.

In a recent development, hong Kong has long been Asia’s biggest art market hub, with headline-grabbing auction sales for over half a century joined, since the 2000s, by a lively landscape of galleries and fairs catering to local collectors, and those from mainland China and the wider region. The city has hosted Art Basel Hong Kong since 2013, and Asian outposts of blue-chip galleries proliferated after the launch of the ArtHK fair in 2008. Artists from the city, however, have struggled to receive much attention in the global market, or even at home.

Leading multinational Western blue-chip galleries such as White Cube, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Gagosian and Pace have shown Asian artists internationally, but they tend to concentrate on bolstering their rosters with established names from Asian cultural powerhouses like mainland China, South Korea and Japan.

Firenze Lai’s A Second Storm (2025) from her White Cube show Photo: © White Cube/Theo Christelis; © the artist.

According to recent reports, hongkonger artists are increasingly exhibiting abroad, but primarily with smaller galleries. The Taipei-based artist Lee Kit works with galleries including Massimo de Carlo in London and ShugoArts in Tokyo. The UK-based Chris Huen Sin-kan revealed with the now-defunct Simon Lee in New York and London, and more recently with Matt Carey-Williams.

Recent findings suggest that while diaspora and émigré Hongkongers have more opportunities to cultivate overseas networks, artists based in the city are also widening their reach. Chang Ya Chin held her first solo show with Perrotin in New York in 2025, while Stephen Wong Chun-hei exhibited with Unit London in 2022 and Mother’s Tankstation in 2025, which also represents Lee Kit. The sound artist Samson Young performed his work Canon at Art Basel Unlimited in 2016, presented by Cologne’s Galerie Gisela Capitain and the now-closed Team Gallery. Wong Ping held a solo show at Tanya Bonakdar Gallery in New York in 2021, while Mak2 had her European gallery solo debut in 2023 with the now-defunct Peres Projects in Berlin.

In a recent development, however, representation by one of the global “massive five” galleries remains rare for Hong Kong artists. White Cube began working with Lai in July 2025. “Her paintings have a singularity that speaks to the human condition, a universal theme that audiences everywhere can appreciate,” a spokesperson for the gallery claims.

Lai was born and raised in Hong Kong, and has lived in London since 2022. Her visual language nonetheless remains rooted in her lived experience of her densely populated hometown. “We are not 100% Chinese, nor are we 100% British,” Lai states.

Industry observers note that moving to London changed how she approaches the canvas. The painter recalls that during her time in Hong Kong—where she built a solid career and a following for her dreamlike figurative paintings through a long-term and continuing collaboration with Guangzhou gallery Vitamin Creative Space—she tended to work on smaller canvases.

“After moving to London, I felt that I needed a bigger canvas. I have a lot more to say,” Lai states. Much of her poignant new work draws from deep emotional responses to her changing environment before and after relocating.

According to recent reports, lai says the current timing for global market recognition for Hong Kong artists makes sense. Those of her generation, born between the late 1970s and 90s, needed time to establish themselves and explore which galleries would be a good fit for their career. “I am proud of the fact that Hong Kong has produced a generation of artists who can have solo demonstrates in London,” she says. “I’ve been told to give up many times. But I can now tell a 15-year-old [aspiring artist] that this is possible.”.

Recent findings suggest that it remains unclear how much long-term benefit a solo exhibition at a global gallery can bring to an artist’s career. “Who are the people paying attention to Firenze right now? If they are private collectors, who are they and what are their demographics? If it’s an institution, who are they?” Ooi asks. Expanding the following for her work will take time as much as exposure.

Sources indicate that lin claims Lai’s move to London put her into a different art world, where she offers galleries a “compelling combination”. “She already comes with a collector base in Asia, an institutional history and more than a decade of critical exposure,” Lin says. “It’s not simply about bringing in Asian collectors, but about adding an artist who connects different collectors, institutional and geographical systems. For a global gallery today, geography can still be a useful entry point, but it cannot be the final framework.”.

Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep

📅 12 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if getting better sleep depends not just on how much you exercise, but how often you move?
  • The findings suggest that consistency could be an important but often overlooked part of the relationship between exercise and sleep.
  • Industry observers note that the study, published in the Journal of Physical Activity & Health, examined activity and sleep data collected from University of Texas students who wore Fitbit devices over several months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if getting better sleep depends not just on how much you exercise, but how often you move? Research from The University of Texas at Austin suggests that being physically active every day, even for short periods, may help people spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep that support recovery, mood, and mental health.

The findings suggest that consistency could be an important but often overlooked part of the relationship between exercise and sleep. Rather than saving all their workouts for the weekend, people may benefit from making movement a regular part of their daily routines.

Industry observers note that the study, published in the Journal of Physical Activity & Health, examined activity and sleep data collected from University of Texas students who wore Fitbit devices over several months. While previous studies have largely examined how much time people spend exercising, the researchers focused on a different question: Does the number of days someone exercises influence how well they sleep?

Sources indicate that "We wanted to know whether it matters if someone spreads out their exercise over the week versus doing it all at once, like a 'weekend warrior,'" said Benjamin Baird, a research assistant professor of psychology in UT Austin's College of Liberal Arts. "And for sleep health, frequency does seem to matter.".

Just 10 Minutes of Daily Exercise May Improve Deep Sleep.

The researchers found that participants who exercised more frequently tended to experience more restorative sleep. The findings build on previous research connecting physical activity with non-REM sleep, a stage that includes the deep sleep essential for physical recovery and healthy brain function.

Chris Corral, who recently earned a master's degree in health behavior and health education from UT Austin and co-led the study, explained that deep sleep is especially important during the early hours of the night. During this period, the body carries out many of the processes that help it recover from the day's physical and mental demands.

Participants who were active more often spent more time in these valuable stages of sleep.

"That's exactly what you want," Baird stated.

"Better sleep means better brain health and potentially lower risks of chronic disease and depression.".

Industry observers note that one particularly encouraging finding was how little exercise appeared to be necessary. Among the young adults studied, as little as 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity per day was associated with better sleep.

Industry observers note that that level of effort does not require an exhausting workout. According to the researchers, moderate to vigorous activity involves breathing harder than usual while still being able to carry on a conversation. On a scale of 1 to 10, the effort would feel like approximately a 6.

Even gentler movement appeared to offer benefits. Regular walking and taking breaks from sitting to stand were also associated with healthier sleep patterns and a more positive mood the following day.

Better Sleep Linked to Improved Mood and Energy.

The potential benefits extended beyond what happened during the night. Participants who exercised more regularly also tended to feel more energetic and experience less stress the next day.

"We saw that more non-REM sleep was tied to better next-day mood and energy," Baird noted.

Industry observers note that this connection is notable because sleep affects far more than whether someone feels rested in the morning. Deep sleep helps the brain and body recover, supporting processes involved in memory, emotional regulation, and overall health.

Previous research has repeatedly linked physical activity with improved sleep, while better sleep itself is associated with greater well-being. However, many earlier investigations took place in controlled laboratories and examined relatively brief periods, sometimes measuring the effects of exercise over a single night.

The UT Austin team wanted to understand how these relationships played out under ordinary living conditions, where exercise habits, sleep schedules, and daily activities can vary considerably.

It has been revealed that to accomplish this, the researchers used wearable fitness trackers to collect information over several months. The Fitbit data allowed them to compare participants' movement habits with their sleep patterns over time, offering a more detailed picture of how everyday activity relates to sleep quality and next-day mood.

Although the findings reveal meaningful associations, the observational approach does not establish that exercising more frequently directly causes improvements in sleep.

Why Daily Exercise May Be Better Than Weekend Workouts.

The results also raise questions about how people should organize their exercise routines.

Recent findings suggest that current recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization call for approximately 150 minutes of moderate physical activity each week. However, those recommendations do not require people to distribute their activity evenly across the seven days.

For some, meeting a weekly exercise target means taking long walks or completing challenging workouts on Saturday and Sunday. Others prefer shorter sessions spread throughout the week.

The UT Austin findings suggest that the second approach may offer particular advantages for sleep, although more research is needed to determine whether daily activity is better than completing an equivalent amount of exercise on fewer days.

"Our results suggest that daily movement may be better for sleep than doing it all on the weekend," Corral stated.

If further studies confirm the importance of exercise frequency, the findings could eventually influence how public health organizations advise people to stay active.

"Current guidelines don't reflect the importance of frequency for sleep health," Baird mentioned. "Having this kind of data allows us to start thinking about whether they should.".

What Better Sleep Could Mean for Brain Health.

The possible implications go well beyond feeling more alert after waking up.

During sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions, including strengthening memories and removing waste products that accumulate during waking hours. Healthy sleep is also closely connected with emotional well-being and long-term physical health.

Recent findings suggest that "Sleep is when your brain stores memories, clears waste and resets," Corral explained. "Better sleep means better brain health and potentially lower risks of chronic disease and depression.".

The research is part of UT Austin's Whole Communities -- Whole Health initiative, an interdisciplinary program that works with communities to investigate factors influencing health and well-being.

The team is now preparing to examine whether the same patterns appear in a larger and more diverse population through the Whole Communities -- Whole Health five-year cohort study. This next phase will help researchers determine whether the findings extend beyond college students to people of different ages and physical activity levels.

For now, the results point toward an accessible way to potentially improve sleep: Make physical activity a regular part of everyday life.

Rather than focusing exclusively on long workouts or ambitious fitness goals, people may benefit from finding small opportunities to move throughout the day. A brief exercise session, a walk, or simply getting up regularly instead of remaining seated may all contribute to healthier routines.

"You don't need to run marathons," Corral remarked. "Just moving a little each day helps. Light activity counts too. Doing something is better than doing nothing.".
