Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain.
  • Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain.
  • According to recent reports, according to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.

According to recent reports, according to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.

Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.

Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self.

The upcoming study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).

Sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.

The researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.

The findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.

Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain.

To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.

Sources indicate that each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.

The team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.

Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.

When movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.

The researchers also identified several other key patterns:.

Together, these findings provide newly introduced evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.

Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain.

According to recent reports, during ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.

But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.

According to recent reports, "In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," said corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are.".

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.

Sources indicate that for someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.

Sources indicate that "The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain.".

This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.

A Newly introduced Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment.

Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.

Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.

Recent findings suggest that "Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity.".

The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.

Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.

In a recent development, both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.

"These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan mentioned. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life.".

Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?

Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.

According to recent reports, mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.

The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.

Zeidan's laboratory is presently conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.

According to recent reports, although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.

Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.

Industry observers note that funding was provided in part by the National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The researchers reported no conflicts of interest.

#45822. How India Is Embracing Social-Emotional Learning

How India Is Embracing Social-Emotional Learning

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When educators feel emotionally and physically supported, they’re in a much better position to support their students.
  • India’s education system comprises over 1 million government schools and more than 82,000 government-aided institutions.
  • The 2020 National Education Policy calls social-emotional learning (SEL) “a critical aspect of any student’s holistic development.” That’s supported by the National Curriculum Framework, which recognizes the importance of fostering stronger student-teacher relationships to accomplish this approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When educators feel emotionally and physically supported, they’re in a much better position to support their students. In India, where the relationship between teacher and student has long been central to education, caring for teachers is essential to sustaining that connection.

India’s education system comprises over 1 million government schools and more than 82,000 government-aided institutions. Serving approximately 167 million children, India administers the world’s largest education system. Increasingly, educators around the world recognize that social-emotional skills like navigating conflict and building healthy relationships are just as essential as academic learning—and India’s own national policies have begun to reflect that shift.

The 2020 National Education Policy calls social-emotional learning (SEL) “a critical aspect of any student’s holistic development.” That’s supported by the National Curriculum Framework, which recognizes the importance of fostering stronger student-teacher relationships to accomplish this approach.

Industry observers note that aditi Ramanthan, a high school biology teacher with almost 20 years of experience, has seen the shift toward more thoughtful discussion and implementation of SEL throughout her time teaching. However, as SEL becomes a more important part of education, the question is not only how to support students, it’s how to support the teachers who are being asked to help them develop these skills.

From this perspective, the future of teaching in India may not be defined only by newly introduced curricula or digital tools, but by whether schools can become places where the hearts of teachers are systematically cared for, so they can, in turn, care for the hearts of children.

“The primary need is psychological safety,” says Ramanathan. “Instead of constantly viewing teachers as being emotionally self-sufficient, creating a space where they can ask for help.”.

In recent years, SEL implementation in India has been widely championed and led by school counselors, with educators throughout grade levels recognizing it as something that should be on par with academic curriculum.

“In India, social-emotional learning is just beginning to come into focus,” says Ramanathan. “Until recently, it wasn’t really part of mainstream conversations in schools, but now we’re starting to talk about it more seriously.”.

Recent findings suggest that ramanthan argues that while SEL has become more widely accepted in recent years, it should be treated as a basic professional requirement for teachers, much like first-aid training, if it’s to be successfully implemented in schools. While schools routinely prepare educators to respond to physical emergencies, far less attention is given to the emotional crises that are likely to unfold in their classrooms. She suggests that SEL training should be universal for teachers, equipping them to understand and respond to students’ inner lives, not just their academic performance.

According to recent reports, “We are not trained for SEL, and I wish we were,” indicates Ramanthan. “We’re given first aid training, but we are not given SEL training, and I think all of us should do SEL training.”.

In a former position, Vrinda Loiwal, founder of the Center for Social Emotional Learning, designed SEL assessments for students, primarily in government-run schools. Once every three months, she would enter classrooms across the country to see how SEL was being interpreted, taught, and assessed.

“One of the challenges to children’s well-being is that even if you teach one SEL standalone lesson once a week, it has to be embodied in the math class, and the English class, and on the playground, and in the messaging all around the students,” Loiwal states. “I believe that there’s very little impact that can come with just a standalone lesson.”.

In a recent development, inconsistency is another challenge. Loiwal explains that about a decade ago, the Delhi school district adopted a latest SEL program—and after years of teacher training and evaluation, they had evidence that what they were doing was working. However, in recent years with a new government in place, the program was scrapped and replaced.

While on paper these new policies tick all the boxes for SEL implementation, when it comes to policy, introducing new required methods every few years disrupts the system just as educators begin to find their footing. They are constantly forced to recalibrate their entire approach, which creates an immense amount of pressure on the educators who are already overwhelmed and stretched thin for time.

“All the teacher training now has to happen all over again and in a slightly latest way because now there’s a new curriculum,” claims Loiwal. “We all agree that you have to teach addition and subtraction in math, but we don’t yet all agree that we have to teach SEL skills or build SEL cultures. These are early efforts, and they’re building. Then the politics change and it feels like two steps forward, one step back.”.

At the Kaveri Group of Institutes in Pune—which includes schools that range from elementary to graduate level—leaders see the strain up close. Teachers are being asked to carry the weight of being disciplinarians, counselors, curriculum experts, and cultural bridges with no real pause in the day to breathe or reflect.

According to recent reports, “An educator is expected to teach, educate, to discipline, to mold the child, to develop the child, to understand the parents, different stakeholders, all of that,” states Deepa Kajale, a consultant for Kaveri. “It’s really overwhelming for the educator to put up with all these kinds of responsibilities.”.

Kajale is a play- and arts-based therapist and school psychologist who has worked with many interventions and iterations of SEL frameworks to foster inclusive, emotionally safe environments. While policymakers are increasingly viewing SEL as essential and not optional, Kajale and her colleagues at Kaveri are attempting to bridge the gap between newly required written frameworks and implementation.

For example, at the Kaveri Gifted Education and Research Center—which aims to identify and nurture gifted students across India—school counselors offer confidential spaces for teachers to talk about both professional and personal struggles like burnout and family stress, and they encourage educators to speak with counselors as a form of ongoing support, rather than viewing reaching out as a last resort.

Devasena Desai, Associate Director for Kaveri Counseling, Empowerment and Gifted Unit since 2014, claims that in addition to offering wellness sessions where they talk about nutrition and menopause, they also celebrate Teacher’s Day. Each year on September 5, they host a large gathering complete with awards to teachers for creativity and innovation, live music, and loud cheering as colleagues are honored.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Additionally, she states one of the most fruitful decisions they made is to offer outsourced counselors from other districts for their educators to speak to.

“Because sometimes you don’t want to talk to the person whom you bump into every day,” says Desai. “Maybe you’re not comfortable and we want to respect that. There are people who wouldn’t mind and there are some people who wouldn’t want to, so that option is there.”.

Along with this more formal support, Kaveri has built in daily rituals of connection, including listening circles where they talk about how to manage varying responsibilities, as well as more sensitive topics like overload and grief.

“What we have introduced in the last two years is talking about trauma, talking about grief, talking about single parenting, blended families, and how to embrace that,” indicates Desai.

According to a paper published in June of this year that studied SEL in Nagaland, India, successful implementation requires specific teacher and parent engagement as well as dedicated training and resources. Additionally, SEL had to be contextually adapted and culturally aligned with local traditions.

Sources indicate that the team at Kaveri understands the importance of cultural relevance when introducing these practices and often draw on concepts like guru and dharma to restore social meaning to the role of the teacher. The ideal of the teacher as a guru or a guide for both knowledge and character still carries significant cultural weight.

Unfortunately, that ideal can collide with the modern reality of rapid policy shifts, fresh technologies, and a workforce made up largely of women juggling caregiving at home and expanding expectations at work.

“Within the professional identity, there is a personal identity with roles, responsibilities, and a lot to take care of as a woman,” says Kajale. “So that adds up to the emotional exhaustion that an educator goes through.”.

According to recent reports, guru is a Sanskrit word meaning “heavy” or “weighty,” used to describe a spiritual teacher or guide who dispels ignorance and leads a student toward self-realization. Rather than abandon the guru ideal as outdated, Kaveri is reclaiming it for the 21st century by rooting teacher support in Indian knowledge systems. In this model, SEL is not just a borrowed framework or a one-off workshop; it’s woven into listening circles, parenting programs, and grief support; and practiced by using a model of wellness that treats educators as whole human beings—body, breath, mind, and spirit.

“We believe that for the holistic development of a person, you have to be very balanced with all your koshas,” says Malati Kalmadi, secretary of Kannada Sangha Public Trust.

In the Panchakosha model from Vedantic philosophy, there are five koshas—or the “five layers of human existence”—including the Annamaya (physical), Pranamaya (energetic), Manomaya (psychological), Vigynamaya (intellectual), and Anandamaya (spiritual). This holistic journey begins with the Annamaya Kosha, focusing on our physical essence through the food we consume. Beyond the visible body lies the Pranamaya Kosha, the vital energy that governs our internal systems—respiratory, circulatory, and nervous.

Achieving equilibrium in these physical and energetic layers is the foundation for mastering the Manomaya Kosha, or the mind. The Vijnanamaya Kosha connects us to our intellect and discernment, while the Anandamaya Kosha is our innermost peace.

Unlike Western perspectives that often separate diet from cognition, the Panchakosha model believes that the food we eat deeply influences the nature of our thoughts, inextricably linking our physical choices to our emotional and mental clarity.

According to recent reports, parents play a vital role in supporting this intentional shift back toward traditional models; Kaveri is working to more deliberately support parents in lifting these inherent values. In addition to the Mindful Parenting Program Workbook they created in collaboration with the Greater Good Science Center’s Parenting Program, they have taken it upon themselves to create additional parenting modules to help parents address the evolving cultural landscape and shifts between millennials, Gen-Z, and Generation Alpha.

To help parents, students, and educators align their koshas, they have experts speak to them about how to switch from “fast food” to “slow food,” helping them become more conscious of what they put into their bodies. One of their team members also went to Bangalore for a training on traditional Indian well-being therapies to provide an alternative to Western medicine.

“We feel that once we are able to get all these things into place, then the wisdom and the thoughts actually move towards spirituality,” states Kalmadi. “Our aim is taking the child towards this track for a better society.”.

While there is no single clean-cut path forward to create schools and districts grounded in SEL, educators across India are already showing that change is possible. By caring for teachers as whole people and drawing on both new research and longstanding cultural traditions, schools can create environments where educators feel supported to care for themselves, their students, and one another.

In that sense, the future of SEL in India may begin not with another mandate, but with a growing recognition that when we care for the people who teach, we strengthen the entire educational community.

“There is slowly a conversation happening between parents, and schools, and teachers, which earlier was not happening consciously, but now we are doing it very, very consciously,” states Kalmadi. “This is proving to be very beneficial for the entire educational ecosystem.”.

According to recent reports, emily Brower is the Education Editor at the Greater Good Science Center and an Associate Producer of The Science of Happiness podcast. In her role as Education Editor, she has covered educator well-being around the world, exploring the experiences and challenges of educators in Ukraine, Singapore, and Spain. Previously, as a music and travel journalist, she contributed to publications including Pure Nowhere, Fifty Grande, and KCPR, covering destinations across Southern and Northern California and the Central Coast. Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain.
  • Sources indicate that although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain.
  • Industry observers note that after participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Sources indicate that although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Industry observers note that after participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," states Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake.".

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow.

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

In a recent development, the latest findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Industry observers note that cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain.

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

According to recent reports, the team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

Recent findings suggest that "Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," indicates Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance.".

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study.

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

#45820. Industry News: Are You Making This Common Mistake With Grief?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1466 w)

Industry News: Are You Making This Common Mistake With Grief?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1466 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent years, the language of therapy has moved beyond the clinic and into everyday conversation, giving us new ways to name our inner lives and, at times, new ways to misread them.
  • In grief, we learn quickly which words help and which ones wound.
  • According to recent reports, not all harmful responses to grief sound like clichés, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, the language of therapy has moved beyond the clinic and into everyday conversation, giving us new ways to name our inner lives and, at times, new ways to misread them. Nowhere is this more evident than in how we respond to grief.

In grief, we learn quickly which words help and which ones wound. “At least they lived a long life.” “They wouldn’t want you to be sad.” Most of us recognize these as unhelpful sentiments.

According to recent reports, not all harmful responses to grief sound like clichés, though. Sometimes they arrive dressed in compassion, wrapped in the language of awareness. A friend might say, “This seems to be activating your abandonment wound,” “Maybe this pain is really about your father,” or “Maybe this is more about your unhappiness in your marriage.” The words may be well-intentioned, even psychologically accurate, yet the effect can be deeply unsettling. Instead of feeling seen, we feel studied; instead of comforted, diagnosed.

In a recent development, this dynamic can feel like a kind of gaslighting because the tools and language of healing are used to explain away your emotions instead of tending to them. Unlike gaslighting in the usual sense, it isn’t malicious. It’s the experience of being told what your pain really means instead of having that pain simply met. It is a byproduct of a therapy-literate culture that often privileges interpretation over presence.

In a recent development, for the past several years, I’ve taught death and dying at the university level and led grief retreats. Again and again, I’ve watched grief ease, not when someone explained it, but when someone stayed with it. In what follows, I’ll look at how analysis can crowd out presence, and offer ways to stay with grief, someone else’s or your own, without rushing to interpret it.

Recent findings suggest that when we’re grieving, people want to help, but few things wound more than having sorrow dissected while it’s still unfolding. Well-meaning insight can become a form of distance. A loved one may believe they’re offering understanding when they say, “This loss must be reminding you of when you lost your job,” or “You seem to struggle with change, don’t you?,” yet the grieving heart hears something different: that the pain belongs to something older and is therefore less legitimate.

Industry observers note that both can be true. A new loss often awakens older ones, but truth without warmth is just analysis. The body doesn’t sort its ache into past and present; it simply calls for accompaniment. In one well-known study, holding the hand of a trusted person calmed the brain’s response to threat, no words required. Seeing where a present loss touches earlier wounds can be deeply healing, eventually. But categorizing pain does not lessen the need to feel it.

According to recent reports, we can also engage in this kind of gaslighting internally. Once we have absorbed enough psychological language, we can turn the same clinical lens on ourselves. We catch the echo of a past wound and then scold our grief for being disproportionate. “I’m overreacting,” we tell ourselves. “This is just my old stuff.” “Why can’t I just be happy?” Yet grief does not care how insightfully we label it. It still needs space to breathe. Awareness can be a form of care, but only when it does not rush ahead of the feeling itself. If it becomes a strategy to bypass feeling, our own or another’s, it defeats itself.

It has been revealed that many guests arrive at our retreats saying some version of “I should be over this by now.” Over the days that follow, that urgency to be finished often quiets, not through argument, but because the grief is finally given room. On the last day, they complete a ritual deep in the forest, at a fountain carved with the outline of a family. Around it, they leave rocks painted with the names of the people they’ve lost. The oldest rocks have since faded almost past recognition, the paint softening into a weathered imprint.

I’ve come to see this not as loss, but as integration: the sharp color of a fresh wound, still seeking an explanation, settling into something that no longer needs to announce itself. No one stood over the rocks interpreting them. They simply bore witness. Grief often becomes more endurable in exactly this way: when it is allowed to change shape in the space of time, care, and presence.

These suggestions come from years of sitting with grieving people, and from my own experience of loss. They are less techniques than reminders of what the moment is asking for.

Resist the urge to explain. The interpretive reflex—reaching for meaning, context, or psychological framing—is often a response to our own helplessness in the face of grief’s rawness. Notice when you’re doing it, pause, and return to the simpler question: Can I be here with this person, without needing it to mean something right now?

It has been revealed that let the silence be full rather than empty. Many people fill silence because it feels like abandonment. A silence in which you remain present, your body in the room, your attention undivided, can be the most companioning thing you offer. “I’m here,” said once and then honored, is worth more than 10 minutes of careful insight.

It has been revealed that follow their lead on meaning. If the grieving person begins to find meaning themselves, to name connections, to speak about what this loss is touching in their past, that is theirs to do. Your role is to witness it, not to initiate it. There is a world of difference between meaning that emerges from the griever and meaning that is handed to them. When you catch yourself doing it, try asking a different question: What does this need? Usually the answer is simpler than any interpretation: company, time, permission to be exactly this intense.

In a recent development, if you feel the pull to theorize about someone else’s grief, a few questions can help you track it in time: Am I trying to ease their pain, or my own discomfort with it? Did they ask for insight, or am I offering it uninvited? Have I acknowledged the loss itself, fully, before reaching for what it might mean?

When you’re unsure what to say, three phrases rarely go wrong: “Tell me about them.” “What do you miss most today?” “I’m here.” Each one keeps the person grieving at the center.

Grief has a way of making us distrust our own experience. We begin measuring whether we’re grieving correctly, whether we’ve stayed sad too long or not long enough, or whether the intensity means something beyond the loss itself.

Catch the self-diagnosis. This one is not easy, because the narrating voice sounds so reasonable: “This is really about my mother,” “I’m being too sensitive,” “I’m being disproportionate.” It rarely confirms itself as unkind.

According to recent reports, notice when you’re applying the same analytical approach to yourself that you’d resist from someone else. Then let the intensity of the feeling stand without demanding it justify itself first.

It has been revealed that ask your grief what it needs, not what it means. Meaning can come later, if it comes at all. In the acute moment, the more honest question is practical: You might need rest, someone to call, permission to cancel a initiative. Let the meaning-making wait.

Recent findings suggest that choose your witnesses. Some people simply cannot stay in the uncertainty that grief creates. Their discomfort reveals up as advice, reassurance, or psychological evaluation. It doesn’t make them uncaring. It simply means they may not be the people to rely on in the rawest moments of loss. Notice who can sit in the room without needing to fix or explain, and lean on them more.

In a recent development, insight has a place in grief. In time, many people do come to see how one loss is woven through the others, and that understanding can bring relief. But it tends to arrive on its own schedule, after the pain has been felt and met. Until then, what we can offer, to someone else or to ourselves, is company. The rocks at the fountain didn’t fade because anyone explained them. They faded because they were left where they were, held by time and by the people who stood beside them. Even when a wound is old, the tenderness it requires is always immediate.

Naomi Sanderovsky, Ph.D., is the founder of Luma Via retreats and trainings, and the creator of Living Grief Theory and Felt Sense Dynamics. She has taught world religions, global philosophy, and more recently death and dying at the university level for more than 20 years.

#45819. Breaking: Can Well-Being Give You Two More Years of Life?

Breaking: Can Well-Being Give You Two More Years of Life?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decades of scientific inquiry have found that the quality and length of a person’s life goes up when they experience less depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions.
  • For many, this combination of findings raises a question: “Does human mortality depend on the presence of human happiness and flourishing, or merely on the absence of mental health symptoms or bad feelings?”.
  • That’s what Max Genecov and David S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decades of scientific inquiry have found that the quality and length of a person’s life goes up when they experience less depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions. More recent studies of psychological well-being—also referred to as happiness, flourishing, thriving, or the good life (among other terms)—have been reporting positive links to health and longevity.

For many, this combination of findings raises a question: “Does human mortality depend on the presence of human happiness and flourishing, or merely on the absence of mental health symptoms or bad feelings?”.

That’s what Max Genecov and David S. Yeager explored in a recent meta-analysis, which combined findings from 99 different studies that measured mental health symptoms and conditions, well-being scores, and lifespan. Importantly, all the studies that they drew from used a longitudinal method, which means they took measurements repeatedly over time to explore whether momentary scores or score changes over time (e.g., well-being in early adulthood, or improvement in well-being) correspond with later scores or changes in another factor (such as the age or cause of death).

Well-being is generally understood as a combination of regularly feeling positive emotions, being satisfied with your life, and having a sense of meaning and purpose in life; ill-being reflects frequent and persistent negative emotions, chronic dissatisfaction, and purposelessness.

To get at this question of whether mental ill-being and well-being over time had overlapping, combined, or independent effects on all-cause mortality, Genecov and Yeager used a statistical approach that allowed them to correct for multiple factors under consideration. Their method was able to mathematically enumerate the impact of well-being on mortality while subtracting any coexisting impact of mental health challenges on mortality.

Recent findings suggest that why? Because if well-being and ill-being exist on a continuum, where reducing mental health conditions is ultimately the same as increasing well-being, then subtracting out the effects of ill-being would erase any concurrent benefit of higher well-being to mortality. But, if improving well-being and reducing ill-being independently affect mortality, where deteriorating mental health conditions and rising well-being contribute separately to how long a person lives, then their model would show distinct advantages of higher well-being to longevity above and beyond reducing symptoms of ill-being.

The result? In this study, people with higher-than-average well-being did live longer—and, indeed, this effect occurs above and beyond the lifespan advantages of lower-than-average ill-being. As the researchers sum up their results:.

Sources indicate that people one standard deviation above the average on well-being die at a 14% slower rate than those with average well-being. . . . As a practical reference using death probabilities from a 2020 United States Social Security Administration actuarial life table, a standard deviation increase on well-being corresponds to just under two years of more life for both men and women.

Recent findings suggest that they saw older adults and patient populations with greater well-being live longer, and they also found people living longer who rated high in optimism, life satisfaction, positive emotion, a sense of social support, and purpose in life. This result isn’t fresh in the research, but by looking at the effects of ill-being, they were able to clarify its relationship to well-being and longevity. In fact, Genecov and Yeager found that the lifespan boost documented in their study (which controlled for the possible benefits of alleviating ill-being) was comparable to other studies of well-being and longevity that didn’t control for ill-being. This suggests that prior studies have also been capturing the unique and separate benefit of well-being to health and longevity.

It has been revealed that while easy to grasp why, for example, less chronic stress would lead to better cardiovascular health and so a longer life, it’s not as clear from a scientific perspective why or how better overall well-being could help someone live longer. Right now, we know that optimism, positive emotion, social support, and purpose are associated with a longer life—we’re just not sure why, exactly.

Industry observers note that that said, there are many ways mental well-being could fuel a longer and better life. More optimistic people, for example, tend to make healthier choices around physical exercise and diet, and to not smoke cigarettes. Positive emotions are linked to investing more effort toward and pursuing goals in life. People who score higher on measures of well-being are more socially appealing, generous, and compassionate toward others, and enjoy higher-quality friendships. One of the most famous studies of longevity attributes survival most strongly to supportive social bonds.

While still an emerging science, those findings suggest that well-being and related factors evoke experiences and motivate behaviors that measurably strengthen physical health in life-lengthening ways. While eliminating ill-being may diminish risks, obstacles, and barriers to physical health, fostering well-being may optimize physical systems to enhance stability, efficiency, and strength—both ultimately contributing to longevity but in different, often intersecting, ways.

In a recent development, want to do more to enhance your well-being? The Greater Good Science Center has an entire website dedicated to supporting people who’d like to increase well-being called Greater Good in Action. You can explore and tinker with over 150 well-being–promoting activities, exercises, and practices drawn from published research, join a four-week Pathway to Happiness program, or try the seven-day Substantial JOY project.

Sources indicate that emiliana R. Simon-Thomas, Ph.D., is the science director of the Greater Good Science Center, where she directs the GGSC's research fellowship program and serves as a co-instructor of its Science of Happiness and Science of Happiness at Work online courses.

#45818. Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1577 w)

Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner.
  • Recent findings suggest that remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives.
  • This ability tends to weaken as we grow older.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner. But as you scan the crowded parking lot, a frustrating question comes to mind. Where did you leave your car? You try to picture the spot, but the memory refuses to surface.

Recent findings suggest that remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives. These memories help form the foundation of long-term memory, whether they involve a childhood milestone, such as the first day of elementary school, or something that happened just minutes earlier, like parking your car.

This ability tends to weaken as we grow older. The sights, sounds, and other details associated with past experiences can become increasingly difficult to retrieve. Scientists still do not fully understand why this happens. Although some memory decline is a common part of aging, the changes can become far more severe in people developing Alzheimer's disease.

It has been revealed that A upcoming study from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, offers important clues about what may be happening inside the aging brain. Neuroscientist Omer Sharon and his colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker, discovered a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The findings suggest that tau buildup in the brain's frontal cortex is linked to changes in the coordinated electrical activity that helps preserve memories overnight.

"This is the first time we've shown this relationship between tau and how it messes with memory consolidation by attenuating traveling slow waves that originate in the frontal cortex," said Sharon, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science.

The research was published in Nature Neuroscience.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Store Memories.

Sleep involves several distinct stages, each associated with different patterns of brain activity. Rapid eye movement sleep is particularly recognizable because the eyes move beneath closed eyelids and most dreaming takes place during this stage. However, another stage, known as non-REM sleep, is especially notable for maintaining healthy brain function.

Sources indicate that during this deeper stage of sleep, when dreaming is limited or absent, large groups of neurons briefly become inactive and then active again in a coordinated sequence. These synchronized changes produce slow electrical waves that spread across the brain, typically beginning in the frontal cortex.

"Each slow wave reflects an enormous population of neurons switching off and back on together," Sharon said. "Our study reveals that for memory, it's critical that these events cascade in sequence across large parts of the brain. This coordinated shutdown has been observed only during deep sleep, and may be one reason why we sleep.".

The researchers found that this carefully organized activity becomes less coordinated as tau accumulates in the aging brain. Instead of traveling together across broad regions, the waves become more scattered and cover shorter distances. These changes are associated with weaker memory consolidation, declining cognitive abilities, and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Disrupted Brain Waves.

It has been revealed that to investigate the relationship, the scientists monitored sleeping brain activity using electroencephalograms (EEGs). They compared cognitively healthy young adults in their early 20s with older participants ranging from their mid-60s to mid-70s.

The differences were striking. In younger participants, groups of slow waves moved together across distances roughly equivalent to the width of a hand on the scalp. Among older adults, the waves typically traveled less far and appeared more independently, rather than moving in coordinated groups.

According to recent reports, the team also examined whether these changes were associated with tau accumulation. Working with Dr. William Jagust, a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of public health and neuroscience, the researchers used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to examine the brains of older participants. This imaging technique uses radioactive tracers introduced into the bloodstream to reveal biological activity and the distribution of specific substances.

The scans demonstrated that greater tau buildup in the frontal cortex was associated with a breakdown in the longer traveling waves normally seen during deep sleep.

Importantly, these changes were present in people who had not developed Alzheimer's disease.

"These people did not have Alzheimer's," Sharon mentioned. "They had tau in their brains, but with subclinical impacts. Their memory decline was within the normal range for their age.".

Sources indicate that sharon explained that early Alzheimer's related changes can vary considerably in severity. The amount of tau present in the brain is associated with cognitive performance, even when a person's memory abilities remain within the expected range for their age.

Mysterious "Lonely Waves" Linked to Memory Loss.

The researchers wanted to determine whether the altered sleep patterns were associated with actual differences in how well people remembered information.

To test this, participants learned pairs of associated words in the evening. The following day, they were asked to recall what they had learned, allowing the scientists to evaluate how effectively the memories had been retained overnight.

Industry observers note that participants whose slow brain waves traveled shorter distances and appeared more isolated generally remembered fewer word associations. The researchers called these disconnected patterns "lonely waves.".

The team also tracked a subset of participants over several years to see how their brains changed with time. Among those whose frontal cortex tau levels increased, the slow waves became less coordinated, and their ability to retain newly learned information overnight declined.

It has been revealed that these observations provide evidence of a relationship between tau accumulation, changes in deep sleep brain activity, and worsening episodic memory. However, they do not establish that tau buildup directly causes memory loss or that disrupted waves are the mechanism responsible.

Additional Tests Strengthen the Connection.

Because PET scans are costly and require specialized facilities, the scientists sought another way to investigate the relationship between Alzheimer's related proteins and sleep activity.

According to recent reports, they collaborated with neurologist Yo-El Ju at Washington University in St. Louis to analyze spinal fluid from a separate group of older adults. The goal was to determine whether measurements of Alzheimer's associated proteins would reveal patterns similar to those seen with brain imaging.

Unlike PET scans, the spinal fluid measurements could not identify tau accumulation specifically within the frontal cortex. Nevertheless, the results pointed in the same direction.

People whose sleeping brains produced more isolated slow waves had higher ratios of tau to amyloid, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, in their spinal fluid.

The consistency between these independent groups and testing methods strengthened the researchers' confidence in the findings.

"It's collected in a totally different place and in a different cohort, so I think that adds to the strength of the evidence," Sharon said.

Together, the sleep recordings, brain scans, spinal fluid analyses, and memory assessments suggest that tau accumulation is associated with a particular disruption of brain activity during deep sleep.

"This longitudinal correlation suggests that Alzheimer's disease pathology is associated with a disruption of this main sleep feature," Sharon said.

What Deep Sleep Reveals About the Aging Brain.

Sources indicate that although memory often declines with age, the newly introduced research indicates that the process may involve more than simply growing older. Changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, particularly tau accumulation in regions responsible for generating widespread slow waves, may help explain why some people experience greater difficulty retaining memories.

Recent findings suggest that "It's not just about age," Sharon noted. "It's how much pathology you have in frontal areas where global waves originate.".

Industry observers note that sleep quality also appears to be part of the picture. Although it can be difficult to define or measure precisely, the organization and movement of slow brain waves may provide notable indicators of how effectively the brain performs its nighttime memory functions.

According to recent reports, the findings raise the possibility that changes in deep sleep activity could eventually help researchers better understand or identify early memory problems. They also point toward potential targets for future treatments aimed at protecting memory as people age.

Recent findings suggest that for now, however, a central question remains unanswered. Scientists still need to determine whether accumulating tau contributes to the breakdown of synchronized sleep waves, whether changes in those waves influence tau accumulation, or whether the relationship involves additional processes.

"We can see tau and lonely waves rising together over time," Sharon said. "What we cannot yet say is which leads -- and that question will shape how we design interventions.".

The study's additional co-authors include Xi Chen, James Westphal, Chelsea Brown, and Vyoma D. Shah of UC Berkeley, along with Jason Dude of Washington University in St. Louis.

Funding came from grants awarded by the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health. Sharon also received support through a Glenn Foundation for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship and a Weill Neurohub Fellowship.

How Couples Create Their Own Unique Microcultures

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that do you have a pet name for your partner?
  • Industry observers note that using pet names is just one example of what some researchers refer to as “microculture”—a combination of shared language, rituals, stories, histories, and more that evolve between small groups of people in close relationships and help sustain them.
  • “People experience this commonly, and our initial research suggests that it’s super pervasive,” says Rossignac-Milon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that do you have a pet name for your partner? I do, and many people I know do, too. Calling your loved one by a special nickname imbued with meaning—like “Bunny,” “Lumba,” or “Buncakes”—communicates in shorthand your unique connection and relational history.

Industry observers note that using pet names is just one example of what some researchers refer to as “microculture”—a combination of shared language, rituals, stories, histories, and more that evolve between small groups of people in close relationships and help sustain them. Maya Rossignac-Milon of Barcelona’s IESE Business School and her research collaborators are looking into how microculture could play a role in the very smallest of groups, romantic couples, and whether it holds clues to how these relationships thrive over time.

“People experience this commonly, and our initial research suggests that it’s super pervasive,” says Rossignac-Milon. “We are basically proposing that attraction and, more importantly, relationship satisfaction is something that’s created together in the moment.”.

While much relationship research focuses on how individual traits (like extraversion, emotional expressiveness, or attachment style) affect relationship dynamics, Rossignac-Milon and her colleagues suggest that the development of microculture also plays an key part in couple formation, happiness, and relationship satisfaction.

Recent findings suggest that “Two people can be quite different from each other, but, with microculture, they’re building something together that didn’t exist before their relationship, that’s totally unique to the two of them,” indicates Rossignac-Milon. “And it’s that process of cocreation that can be really powerful.”.

When people fall in love, they start merging their identities in certain ways and expanding their sense of self to include the other person. Creating a special microculture, consisting of inside jokes, pet names, repeated stories, and more, is one way couples cement their special connection.

Industry observers note that what does this look like in practice? Rossignac-Milon says there are three core factors that move everyday interactions into the realm of microculture:.

All three of these should be present for something to be part of your microculture. Consider this example. Every year, some friends of mine celebrate “the miracle of the tent,” a playful reference to the moment their platonic friendship turned unexpectedly romantic. Imbued with humor and meaning, this idiosyncratic holiday is part of their microculture, reinforcing their unique bond over time.

In a recent development, shared origin stories are a common way that couples create microculture, helping to sustain their relationship. When they reminisce about turning points in their relationship and share their story with others, it can increase relationship satisfaction, research suggests. Couples who initiate nostalgic recollections of past shared experiences feel closer to their partners and are more committed. Perhaps that’s why my husband Don and I like to prompt people to share their origin story when meeting them for the first time. (Not to mention, they often ask us to return the favor—a win-win!).

In a recent development, inside jokes can also express a couple’s microculture. For example, Don once bought me a t-shirt that he promised to wear with the words, “You’re right, dear,” printed on the front. I immediately got the joke—a humorous acknowledgment of times he’d insisted he was right about something when he wasn’t. Now it’s become a much-used catchphrase for admitting our mistakes. (He needs to say it more often than I do, of course).

In a recent development, relationship rituals can also be part of your unique microculture if they are symbolically meaningful (and not just routine). Bringing coffee to your wife in bed on a silver tray might be your tongue-in-cheek way of acknowledging that she’s not a morning person and needs princess pampering. Or eating at the same Italian restaurant the first Friday of every month might be a nod to how you fell in love there over a plate of spaghetti. These small rituals communicate shared history and meaning, helping couples feel part of something special.

My colleague Katherine and her husband Brian developed a shorthand for recognizing moments when their dual-career family feels stretched thin. If either one needs to work late, instead of expressing frustration or being passive-aggressive, the other one says, “Thank you for doing that for our family.” This acknowledges that, while each of them would prefer to be relaxing with their kids and spouse, duty calls, and they’re doing the best they can to manage their work demands.

Industry observers note that shared language, stories, and rituals are often the most visible aspects of microculture, says Rossignac-Milon. But, just like macrocultures, microcultures also involve a shared sense of identity, morality, and reality.

Romantic partners tend to form identities as a couple that are distinct from their individual identities and serve to strengthen their relationship. For example, they may consider themselves to be “cat people” or a “power couple.” When partners are clear about their identity as a couple, it’s tied to higher levels of commitment.

It has been revealed that having a shared moral code (shared values and norms) is also part of a couple’s microculture. This might include rules like never working on Sundays, requiring both people to apologize after a conflict, or being sexually exclusive on weekends only. If broken, these norms may elicit anger, hurt, or the need to repair; so, the extent to which they are agreed upon and easily managed strengthens a couple’s well-being.

According to recent reports, A shared sense of reality supports couples in their relationship, too. In a study run by Rossignac-Milon and her colleagues, they found that couples who perceive an overlap in how they view the world with their partner feel less uncertainty and more meaning in life than if they think their partner diverges from their worldview. When experiments manipulate a couple’s sense of agreement on their perceptions to signal disagreement, the researchers found, couples will try to compensate by leaning more heavily on shared microcultural references, as if to repair the rift in their shared reality.

“People really care about this experience, and when it’s threatened, they want to protect their sense of, ‘No, we do have our own shared culture that we’ve developed together,’” indicates Rossignac-Milon.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

While aspects of microculture within couples have mostly been described theoretically by drawing on past research, Rossignac-Milon and her colleagues have begun to research the overall concept more empirically, too.

It has been revealed that in a currently unpublished study, she and her collaborators asked couples from diverse backgrounds to list three examples of each potential element of their microculture—from shared language to shared reality. Then, the couples kept daily diaries for two weeks, where they reported any references to their microculture that day and their feelings about their relationship. The researchers found that couples were happier with their relationship on days when their microculture was referenced more than usual. Also, looking at patterns across couples, those who referenced their microculture more were more satisfied with and committed to their relationship than those who referenced it less.

“People who tend to have more microculture and use it more are happier in their relationships and are more connected to and committed to their partners across the board,” says Rossignac-Milon.

Though microculture may help couples feel more connected and committed, there can be dark sides to the phenomenon, too, claims Rossignac-Milon. Just like how some macrocultural norms and behaviors can make groups more insular or encourage shared false beliefs, microcultures can sometimes become problematic.

Industry observers note that for example, sharing perceptions or beliefs with your partner may increase your certainty in your viewpoint and boost your convictions, perhaps in a way that isolates you from others, says Rossignac-Milon. Similarly, you can sometimes reinforce unhealthy behaviors, like encouraging each other to smoke if you identify as a couple that smokes together, health risks be damned.

A more extreme example might be how microculture can develop into a shared psychosis or support abusive relationships, claims Rossignac-Milon.

“If the rituals and norms that people establish together are toxic to begin with or have power dynamics that are fostering inequality and an asymmetry in the relationship, that can be dangerous,” she says. This suggests that couples should pay attention to any darker aspects of microculture that could have these nefarious effects.

Industry observers note that on the plus side, knowing the importance of microculture in romantic relationships can help people make dating more productive, says Rossignac-Milon. Instead of just looking for “Mr. or Ms. Right”—someone who checks off your boxes in terms of traits you want in a partner—pay attention to what’s created between you when spending time together. That playful banter or those surprising connections are part of what makes people feel like they click.

“Microculture is all about the experience of interacting and creating inside jokes and ways of using words that you have together and matter so much,” says Rossignac-Milon. “Letting yourself lean into that and using that as a diagnostic cue could be one important signal of compatibility that people are not always attending to.”.

In a recent development, to encourage more of that special connection, she suggests taking small risks and not just saying what you think is expected of you. Those little idiosyncrasies or moments of vulnerability can serve to attract someone to you more than what’s on their resume.

According to recent reports, “Put yourself out there and use a funny word or do something that’s a little bit different from what others might do,” she suggests. “Those are the things that can easily turn into inside jokes and microculture that you can reference back to.”.

In a recent development, couples in ongoing relationships can also benefit from paying attention to their microculture, she adds. It’s sometimes more natural to do that early on in a relationship and then neglect it over time. But continuing to reference your microculture and building on it is a way of keeping your relationship strong.

“The more that people can keep growing their microculture, the more they can continue to reap those relational benefits,” states Rossignac-Milon.

To nurture your microculture, it’s helpful to keep a spirit of joint creativity alive in your relationship and to introduce fresh experiences, inside jokes, rituals, and more. Otherwise, they can get old and stop having the same beneficial effect—similar to the way jokes can get stale and less funny over time, says Rossignac-Milon.

On the other hand, there’s no need to put pressure on yourself, either, she says. Building rapport through microculture is something that anyone can do, regardless of who you are.

“Jointly riffing, this kind of playful cocreation, may be something that some people are naturally good at, but it’s also a skill that can be developed by anyone, as long as they’re coming into it with spontaneity and a willingness to be a little bit vulnerable.”.

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

Latest Update: Artist captures the saga of Luigi Mangione in tweets

  • “The compression of anger and joy that I was seeing people write that day was astonishing,” Kahn tells The Art Newspaper; she immediately felt compelled to capture the torrent of reactions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the morning of 4 December 2024, the Los Angeles-based artist Stanya Kahn opened X (formerly Twitter) to get her daily news digest, when she, like many Americans, was inundated with a mass chorus of tweets—ranging from celebratory snark to unbridled vitriol—about the assassination of United HealthCare’s chief executive Brian Thompson.

“The compression of anger and joy that I was seeing people write that day was astonishing,” Kahn tells The Art Newspaper; she immediately felt compelled to capture the torrent of reactions. “At first I was bookmarking them, and then [screenshotting] them, and fairly swiftly my thought was to gather these up because the algorithm might start shutting them down.”.

Fairly swiftly, the Trump administration announced that any celebration of the killing could be criminalised. But with an ever-growing archive and a long-held practice as a time-based media artist, Kahn decided to create a film that chronologically presented the public’s rapidly unfolding response to this now-infamous event.

Flyer for Deny, Defend, Depose (2026) Courtesy of Stanya Kahn.

Titled Deny Defend Depose (2026)—a play on the words scrawled on three shell casings from bullets fired in the shooting, and the strategy invoked by major healthcare providers to reduce payouts and increase profits—Kahn’s film is now screening across the country at artist-run-spaces, cinemas and galleries. The Fresh York non-profit space Participant Inc will screen it on 13 November, with more showings to come.

Industry observers note that originally, Kahn planned to release the film in the lead-up to 9 September, when the state trial of Luigi Mangione was due to take place in Upcoming York. Now that Mangione’s 14 August guilty plea—an attempt to avoid double jeopardy—has postponed the state hearing until 10 December, with a federal hearing to follow on 18 December, Kahn plans to continue updating the film with more responses from the public as the saga continues.

Sources indicate that when it all began, she had considered turning the project into a coffee-table book, which would afford a funny inversion of X’s quippy, short-form format. But switching to a film, her primary medium, afforded an opportunity for in-person film screenings, which enabled the originally solitary experience of watching the commentary unfold online to be transformed into a collective viewing experience.

Stanya Kahn, Deny, Defend, Depose (2026, still), 30:28 min Courtesy of the artist.

According to recent reports, set to a dramatic soundtrack of acid and jungle, the 30-minute film takes viewers on an emotional rollercoaster. Watching the tweets unfold in sequence together, the audience collectively holds its breadth as anticipation builds to the moment the suspect is revealed as Mangione, laughs as tweets comment on his attractiveness or the Monopoly money found in his backpack, and sighs at the devastating state of healthcare in the United States when statistics regarding industry salaries and investment patterns, or personal anecdotes about life-threatening denials, are shared.

Sources indicate that just like Kahn was glued to X that morning in late 2024, viewers of her film are often transfixed as they relive their reactions to the still-unfolding story at top speed.“The poignancy of such a broad spectrum of the American public responding in kind to what was basically a public political assassination felt like a rupture, especially in party-based politics,” Kahn says. “It cut across the entire political spectrum and the common ground that suddenly emerged in this flashpoint seemed like a upcoming beacon for potential mass movement, because it was a unity that emerged spontaneously and instantaneously, it wasn’t something that got hammered out in time.”.

In a recent development, the outpouring of affection for Mangione has been staggering, Kahn notes. “Without blinking,” she adds, “people were in full-throat applause of [an alleged] murderer.”.

Stanya Kahn, Deny, Defend, Depose (2026, still), 30:28 min Courtesy of the artist.

Attention from the media and public has remained steady since the early days of the manhunt, Mangione’s arrest and the trial, with comparisons to Robin Hood, lookalike contests and wanted posters for other healthcare company executives. While the extent of the public’s celebration of Thompson’s killing took many by surprise, Kahn sees this reaction as evidence of just “how deep the pain and anger and frustration is in this country about the evilness of the healthcare system and its inaccessibility”. (Per capita spending on healthcare in the US is double the average of other wealthy countries, and has been increasing faster than inflation for decades.).

It has been revealed that thompson’s killing and its aftermath are hardly a black-and-white tale of righteous moral vengeance. Though some originally attempted to paint Mangione as disaffected and radicalised, his Ivy League education and privileged upbringing told a different story. And the responses to the event “weren’t just coming from more radical spaces”, Kahn says. While capturing their reactions in real time and reviewing the posters’ profiles, she found, “it was literally just ‘every man’—people with five followers and five million. It was regular people because they were pissed.”.

#45814. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
